Paralympic Heroes [4881]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Paralympic

While the Olympics celebrate the pinnacle of athletic acumen, the Paralympics’ athletic achievement is testament to the tenacity of the human spirit.

South Africa won a total of 17 medals, 7 of them gold and their achievements are nothing short of heroic.

I have chosen 3. Kevin Paul Silver for swimming, Tyrone Pillay, bronze for shot put and Ntando Mahlangu silver for 200m.

I think everyone wants to find out more about Ntando. A boy who is still in primary school and who only started walking 4 years ago. He is connected to a charity called Jumping Kids which creates prosthetics for children with disabilities. His coach is the physio from this organisation, she herself is an amputee and has represented South Africa in equestrian events. Like Wayde Van Niekerk’s coach she is in her late 60’s.
They will let me know tomorrow whether we can film them in Pretoria.

Here are brief biographies of the 3.
We will pick up short interviews of the others at the airport tomorrow morning when Mark and Sinethemba will go and film welcoming event.

Kevin Paul won Gold in the 100m breastroke in a time of 1min 04.86sec. This was his second Paralympic gold medal after doing the same in Beijing eight years ago. In London four years ago‚ Paul had to settle for silver in his keynote event.
His winning time is only 6 seconds slower than the Olympic time.
He swims in the SB9 category.
This class describes minimal physical impairments of eligible swimmers. These include the loss of one hand or a movement restriction in one hip joint.
His coach is Graham Hill who coaches Chad Le Clos.

Tyrone Pillay won bronze in shot put with a personal best of 13.91 to claim his countries seventh medal of the Games.

Durban boy Tyrone (34) was born with an abnormality of the left foot which resulted in the need for a prosthetic foot to assist him with walking. He is categorised as an above-knee amputee.
“It’s called Les Autres, which in French means the others. I’ve never seen myself as different though. I thrive on positive thinking. My parents never made a decision to amputate my limb because my father said that when I was old enough, it would be my decision to make. I chose not to have an amputation. This is my life, I don’t know any other way. Irrespective of my disability, I always wanted to be a South African sportsman. As a kid, I used to spend hours in front of the mirror visualising myself at the Olympics, hearing the roaring cheers of supporting crowds. I still have this vision.”
With seven prosthetic legs: one for general walking, one for gym, a running blade, a throwing foot and three backups, Tyrone has strived to live a life as normal as any other. He played cricket for 14 years until his disability prevented him from reaching greater goals in the sport, so he set his sights on making the country proud through disabled athletics.
“When I first got involved it was an eye opener. I had no idea disabled sports was so competitive. It was this awakening that motivated me to better myself and really take the sport seriously.”
While he might be an IT manager for Toyota, when he’s not on the sports field chasing his goal of forming part of the SA Para-Olympic squad, Tyrone works closely with a company called Icexpress Prosthetics who have designed a prosthetic foot that will improve his performances, allowing him the opportunity to compete at the highest level. He is also an ambassador for Jumping Kids Charity which aims to supply the latest in prosthetic limb technology to South African children in need.
“When I lost my father 12 years ago, I realised that I had to help those in need in whatever possible way. My work with Jumping Kids will give children the same opportunity my parents gave me. I know you can overcome anything if you have the will to succeed. In life it’s not only about winning but the fact that you performed your best that counts.”

Ntando Mahlangu
Four years ago, Mahlangu was a ten-year-old who had been confined to a wheelchair pretty much since he was born. He suffered from hemimelia, a condition which meant that his legs didn’t fully develop below the knees. With the help of Jumping Kids, a non-profit organisation which helps fit youngsters with prostheses, Mahlangu was given shiny new cheetah blades.
As he was watching the London 2012 Paralympics, he was just learning to walk again. It took some effort – he needed assistance with learning how to balance, but as with everything Mahlangu has done so far in his young life, he learnt quickly. It took him just five days to master the blades.
“I was just learning to walk (in 2012 during the London Paralympic Games),” Mahlangu told the Paralympic News Service. “I was so excited when I took my first step that I vomited. The guy (doctor) asked me why I vomited and I told him I was so happy. I learnt fast, in about five days.”
Five days after being able to walk, he could run. Since that day, Mahlangu has done nothing but excel.
In 2014, he won gold in the National Athletics Championships and took silver in the long jump to boot. He set three new African records (and unofficial Junior World records) in the T42 under-20 category at the 2015 SASAPD National Athletics Championships and won gold in the javelin item.
He competed against able-bodied athletes and set an unofficial (the record did not stand because it was against able-bodied athletes) senior record in the T42 400m in 2015. This year, he set the 400m T42 World Record (53.19s) to add to his African records in the 100m (13.34s), 200m (26.20s) and, unofficially, the 800m (2:14.00s).
At the 2016 IAWS U23 World Games in June/July this year, he won gold in the T42 200m (25.89s), gold and beat his own world record in the 800m (2:06.70s), he also won gold in the 100m (13.13s), and won gold and beat his own world record in the 400m (52.61s). Before the Olympics, he won silver with a new personal best time of 23.97 at the Muller Anniversary Games in London in July.
The silver at the Paralympics was yet another personal best and another African record, even if the 200m isn’t his preferred race.
It is almost impossible not to be enchanted by this young, beaming, bouncing athlete. Prior to being fitted with prostheses he was in a school for disabled students, but has since moved to a different school – and adapted from English to Afrikaans as a medium of instruction. He dreams of being an engineer one day, because he doesn’t believe athletics should ever be work. He is wise beyond his young years and talented beyond words.

Press Release:


Paralympic Heroes
They’ve returned home from the Rio Games with a total of 17 medals, having excelled in events as varied as swimming, shot-put, running, long jump, javelin and more. Carte Blanche meets the heroic Paralympic athletes who have overcome seemingly insurmountable personal and professional odds to do the nation proud.


Script:


Paralympic Script


V/O
It’s early Tuesday morning and the fans have arrived at OR Tambo International Airport to welcome back home the heroes of the 2016 Paralympic games in Rio.

Up sound jubulation

V/O
Competing against 4000 athletes from 176 countries around the world, South Africa’s team was only 40 strong, but they came back with 17 medals , 7 of them gold.

Minister of Sports
The story of the paralympics is a great story. It’s a story of the triumph of human spirit. It is a story that says to us that you are not disempowered by your disability.

V/O
Twenty five year old paralympian swimmer Kevin Paul was first off the mark. Rio was his 3rd paralympics, he won gold in Beijing and silver in London in the 100m breastroke. He was ranked as the favourite to win.

Kevin
“The first thing I looked at when is my 100 breastroke and I saw it was on day 1 that I would be the first South African competing and I was like inside come on we have got this we can get the ball rolling for South Africa.

V/O
Kevin was born with Poland Syndrome, which means that he is missing muscles on the upper left side of his body. He has been swimming since the age of three.
He’s never seen himself as disabled but as differently abled.

Claire Link
Kevin trains here at Lahee Park in Durban, the same pool where Chad le Clos trained at and their gruelling training regimes are not very different.

Kevin
“I’ve been lucky to train with olympic guys, I am in the water from when they are in the water, I get out when they get out of the water, so I am doing the same amount of work as these guys day in and day out.’

V/O
And Kevin’s complete dedication paid off.

Up Sounds
“Men’s 100m Olympic Footage

V/O
Kevin knew that if he wanted to achieve gold he had to devote himself completely to the training. He left in his final year of his law degree to focus on winning gold.

Kevin
“You’ve trained you’ve made sacrifices , it’s all going to come down to this one moment in your life.

Up Sound
“Who will touch first strokes quickening, Paul goes for gold Kevin Paul of SA 8 years on from winng his first paralympic gold medal has reclaimed the title he lost in london 4 years ago.”

Kevin
‘I went mad I was getting on the lane ropes thanking the crowd.”

“He’s got the gold medal, paralypian champion again”.

Claire Link
Each paralympic medal makes a sound when shakento tell visually impaired athletes what medal they have got. The bronze has 16 balls making the lowest sound, the silver 20 and the gold 28 producing the loudest sound. Each medal also has the words 2016 in braille.

Up sound Anrune Liebenberg is in lane 4
“I have a great passion for it. I love what I do.”
Everytime I run I get goosebumps and my heart beats a little faster.”

V/O
These athletes are testament to the power of human endurance , despite having two knee operations months before Rio, Anrune Liebenberg who was born with a deformed left arm, still won silver.

Up Sound Liebenberg holding on, Liebenberg takes the silver.

Anrune
“We all have disabilities –my favourite movie is Soul Surfer where he says being normal is overrated –this is how life is – we are all different and unique and god made us like that.

V/O
Cerebral palsied Dyan Buis from the Western Cape won two medals the gold in the 400m and a bronze medal in the long jump.

Up Sound
“Buis is going to be the champion.”



Dyan
“I was very emotional when I crossed that line because it has been some times it has been very tough for me I wanted to stop at one stage doing athletics because of some challenges.”

Link
Not only do these paralympians have to deal with the challenges of having a disability they struggle to get the necessary funding and recognition they so deserve.

Dyan
Truth being said that I cannot make a professional career at this stage just doing sport, that is why I have qualified as a teacher and I am still studying.

V/O
There is a risk that these remarkable athletes simply cannot continue to compete and bring home the medals. SASCOC or the South African Sports Confederation and Olympic Committee does support them, but corporate South Africa largely ignores them says Mervyn Paul, Kevin’s father.

Claire
“Do our paralympians get the funding and recognition that that the need?

Mervyn
“Emphatically no definitely not.

V/O
Mervyn contacted 27 potential corporate sponsors for Kevin last year and received no joy.

Mervyn
“The first one said to me that they get no mileage out of these athletes, the second company said he doesn’t meet the criteria he doesn’t meet the criteria.

V/O
Rio was 36 year old Tyrone Pillay’s first paralympics. He is a shot putter and is also affectionately know as the Hulk. He was born with abnormailty of the left foot and is classified as an above the knee amputee. He lives with his family in Durban.

“How did your family deal with Tyrone’s disability?”

Suzy
“When he was born the first day I did cry. Because its emotional, those days disability was something like terrible you know family generally with the indian community. The first doctor we went to he says he has to amputate his leg, now you just have a new baby and they tell you amputate. Oh I was hysterical. That’s nonsense.

V/O
The family decided against amputation and by 10 months old Tyrone was walking with a prosthesis. As a child he had olympic dreams from the age of 3.

Tyrone
“So I used to stand in front of the mirror everyday and think that I was running the relay at the olympics, take a can of deoderant and pass it to myself and just keep running. And I always dreamt of that moment when the crowd would be screaming for you and building up to all of that.So it was something I dreamt about, I did not realise it is something that would happen.I’ll be honest about it”

V/O
Tyrone is largely self funded. He works full time as an IT specialist and trains for 2 hours before and 2 hours after work, 6 days a week.

Suzy
“He’s only home between 9 and half past nine . Very dedicated and the next morning at 5 he starts work again so if somebody deserves I it is hime because he really put in the time.”

Tyrone
“As I got out the ramp and something I wrote on my hand is I love you Rio in portugese and the crowd went balastic and screaming at me and I just love that atmosphere and you feed off thos kind of things.”

V/O
Inspired by the crowds Tyrone put everything behind his last throw.

Tyrone
‘Let’s just go all out now, locked back out shot in my neck and let rip and I did a 13.91 hich turned out to be a new PB , new south african record and african record.

Suzy
That excitement to see him and he pointed to me to say this is for you and I was then I started crying and flag on him simply awesome.

Suzy

“That excitement to see him and he pointed to me

Tyrone’s prize money for winning the bronze medal is R80 000 and he is going to donate it to Jumping Kids an NGO that helps disabled children with prosthetic limbs.

Tyrone
“It’s going to empower them and change their lives dramatically. I think people don’t relise the benefits of prosthetic limbs, on ethey are going to be able to walk and go to normal schooling and they will be self sufficient and I think that key.

V/O
14 year old Ntando Mahlangu from Mpumalanga is one of the people that the charity helped. He was confined to a wheelchair and 4 years ago was given prosthetics and finally learnt to walk for the first time.

NTANDO:
“In 2012 I got a bit interested in sports and I kind of liked sport and that’s where the dream began”

V/O
Four years later Ntando, who is still in primary school, would compete in his first Paralympic Race in Rio – making it to the Men’s 200m Final.

Up sound and away they go

NTANDO:
“I came out of the bend and I was giving all my best. And I was trying to catch the guy but the guy was fast.”

V/O
While the gold medal was just out of Ntando’s reach, he clinched the silver.

NTHANDO:
“It was a vey good competition. And ja, it was a very, very, very good race.”

Kevin
“Every single athlete has a story to tell and it doesn’t matter if you come last or first , just being a Paralympic athlete for team south Africa means that you have won a gold in life.”

Promo 2

NTHANDO:
“It was a vey good competition. And ja, it was a very, very, very good race.”

Promo 3
Opening parade
The Paralympic athletes, laden with medals returned to South Africa to a heroes welcome.

Fikile
It’s a story that says to us you are not disempowered by your disability.”

Claire Link Each paralympic medal makes a sound when shakento tell visually impaired athletes what medal they have got. The bronze has 16 balls making the lowest sound, the silver 20 and the gold 28 producing the loudest sound. Each medal also has the words 2016 in braille. Up sound Anrune Liebenberg is in lane 4 “I have a great passion for it. I love what I do.” Everytime I run I get goosebumps and my heart beats a little faster.” V/O These athletes are testament to the power of human endurance , despite having two knee operations months before Rio, Anrune Liebenberg who was born with a deformed left arm, still won silver. Up Sound Liebenberg holding on, Liebenberg takes the silver. Anrune “We all have disabilities –my favourite movie is Soul Surfer where he says being normal is overrated –this is how life is – we are all different and unique and god made us like that. V/O Cerebral palsied Dyan Buis from the Western Cape won two medals the gold in the 400m and a bronze medal in the long jump. Up Sound “Buis is going to be the champion.” Dyan “I was very emotional when I crossed that line because it has been some times it has been very tough for me I wanted to stop at one stage doing athletics because of some challenges.” Link Not only do these paralympians have to deal with the challenges of having a disability they struggle to get the necessary funding and recognition they so deserve. Dyan Truth being said that I cannot make a professional career at this stage just doing sport, that is why I have qualified as a teacher and I am still studying. V/O There is a risk that these remarkable athletes simply cannot continue to compete and bring home the medals. SASCOC or the South African Sports Confederation and Olympic Committee does support them, but corporate South Africa largely ignores them says Mervyn Paul, Kevin’s father. Claire “Do our paralympians get the funding and recognition that that the need? Mervyn “Emphatically no definitely not. V/O Mervyn contacted 27 potential corporate sponsors for Kevin last year and received no joy. Mervyn “The first one said to me that they get no mileage out of these athletes, the second company said he doesn’t meet the criteria he doesn’t meet the criteria. V/O Rio was 36 year old Tyrone Pillay’s first paralympics. He is a shot putter and is also affectionately know as the Hulk. He was born with abnormailty of the left foot and is classified as an above the knee amputee. He lives with his family in Durban. “How did your family deal with Tyrone’s disability?” Suzy “When he was born the first day I did cry. Because its emotional, those days disability was something like terrible you know family generally with the indian community. The first doctor we went to he says he has to amputate his leg, now you just have a new baby and they tell you amputate. Oh I was hysterical. That’s nonsense. V/O The family decided against amputation and by 10 months old Tyrone was walking with a prosthesis. As a child he had olympic dreams from the age of 3. Tyrone “So I used to stand in front of the mirror everyday and think that I was running the relay at the olympics, take a can of deoderant and pass it to myself and just keep running. And I always dreamt of that moment when the crowd would be screaming for you and building up to all of that.So it was something I dreamt about, I did not realise it is something that would happen.I’ll be honest about it” V/O Tyrone is largely self funded. He works full time as an IT specialist and trains for 2 hours before and 2 hours after work, 6 days a week. Suzy “He’s only home between 9 and half past nine . Very dedicated and the next morning at 5 he starts work again so if somebody deserves I it is hime because he really put in the time.” Tyrone “As I got out the ramp and something I wrote on my hand is I love you Rio in portugese and the crowd went balastic and screaming at me and I just love that atmosphere and you feed off thos kind of things.” V/O Inspired by the crowds Tyrone put everything behind his last throw. Tyrone ‘Let’s just go all out now, locked back out shot in my neck and let rip and I did a 13.91 hich turned out to be a new PB , new south african record and african record. Suzy That excitement to see him and he pointed to me to say this is for you and I was then I started crying and flag on him simply awesome. Suzy “That excitement to see him and he pointed to me Tyrone’s prize money for winning the bronze medal is R80 000 and he is going to donate it to Jumping Kids an NGO that helps disabled children with prosthetic limbs. Tyrone “It’s going to empower them and change their lives dramatically. I think people don’t relise the benefits of prosthetic limbs, on ethey are going to be able to walk and go to normal schooling and they will be self sufficient and I think that key. V/O 14 year old Ntando Mahlangu from Mpumalanga is one of the people that the charity helped. He was confined to a wheelchair and 4 years ago was given prosthetics and finally learnt to walk for the first time. NTANDO: “In 2012 I got a bit interested in sports and I kind of liked sport and that’s where the dream began” V/O Four years later Ntando, who is still in primary school, would compete in his first Paralympic Race in Rio – making it to the Men’s 200m Final. Up sound and away they go NTANDO: “I came out of the bend and I was giving all my best. And I was trying to catch the guy but the guy was fast.” V/O While the gold medal was just out of Ntando’s reach, he clinched the silver. NTHANDO: “It was a vey good competition. And ja, it was a very, very, very good race.” Kevin “Every single athlete has a story to tell and it doesn’t matter if you come last or first , just being a Paralympic athlete for team south Africa means that you have won a gold in life.” Promo 1 10 seconder They’ve returned home from the Rio games with a total of 17 medals. Meet the men and women of team South Africa - the courageous paralympic athletes who have done our nation proud. Promo 2 14 year old running sensation Ntando Mahlangu who only learnt to walk 4 years ago won the silver in 200m at the Rio Paralympics NTHANDO: “It was a vey good competition. And ja, it was a very, very, very good race.” Promo 3 Opening parade The Paralympic athletes, laden with medals returned to South Africa to a heroes welcome. Fikile It’s a story that says to us you are not disempowered by your disability.”

metadata.Further information: Paralympic While the Olympics celebrate the pinnacle of athletic acumen, the Paralympics’ athletic achievement is testament to the tenacity of the human spirit. South Africa won a total of 17 medals, 7 of them gold and their achievements are nothing short of heroic. I have chosen 3. Kevin Paul Silver for swimming, Tyrone Pillay, bronze for shot put and Ntando Mahlangu silver for 200m. I think everyone wants to find out more about Ntando. A boy who is still in primary school and who only started walking 4 years ago. He is connected to a charity called Jumping Kids which creates prosthetics for children with disabilities. His coach is the physio from this organisation, she herself is an amputee and has represented South Africa in equestrian events. Like Wayde Van Niekerk’s coach she is in her late 60’s. They will let me know tomorrow whether we can film them in Pretoria. Here are brief biographies of the 3. We will pick up short interviews of the others at the airport tomorrow morning when Mark and Sinethemba will go and film welcoming event. Kevin Paul won Gold in the 100m breastroke in a time of 1min 04.86sec. This was his second Paralympic gold medal after doing the same in Beijing eight years ago. In London four years ago‚ Paul had to settle for silver in his keynote event. His winning time is only 6 seconds slower than the Olympic time. He swims in the SB9 category. This class describes minimal physical impairments of eligible swimmers. These include the loss of one hand or a movement restriction in one hip joint. His coach is Graham Hill who coaches Chad Le Clos. Tyrone Pillay won bronze in shot put with a personal best of 13.91 to claim his countries seventh medal of the Games. Durban boy Tyrone (34) was born with an abnormality of the left foot which resulted in the need for a prosthetic foot to assist him with walking. He is categorised as an above-knee amputee. “It’s called Les Autres, which in French means the others. I’ve never seen myself as different though. I thrive on positive thinking. My parents never made a decision to amputate my limb because my father said that when I was old enough, it would be my decision to make. I chose not to have an amputation. This is my life, I don’t know any other way. Irrespective of my disability, I always wanted to be a South African sportsman. As a kid, I used to spend hours in front of the mirror visualising myself at the Olympics, hearing the roaring cheers of supporting crowds. I still have this vision.” With seven prosthetic legs: one for general walking, one for gym, a running blade, a throwing foot and three backups, Tyrone has strived to live a life as normal as any other. He played cricket for 14 years until his disability prevented him from reaching greater goals in the sport, so he set his sights on making the country proud through disabled athletics. “When I first got involved it was an eye opener. I had no idea disabled sports was so competitive. It was this awakening that motivated me to better myself and really take the sport seriously.” While he might be an IT manager for Toyota, when he’s not on the sports field chasing his goal of forming part of the SA Para-Olympic squad, Tyrone works closely with a company called Icexpress Prosthetics who have designed a prosthetic foot that will improve his performances, allowing him the opportunity to compete at the highest level. He is also an ambassador for Jumping Kids Charity which aims to supply the latest in prosthetic limb technology to South African children in need. “When I lost my father 12 years ago, I realised that I had to help those in need in whatever possible way. My work with Jumping Kids will give children the same opportunity my parents gave me. I know you can overcome anything if you have the will to succeed. In life it’s not only about winning but the fact that you performed your best that counts.” Ntando Mahlangu Four years ago, Mahlangu was a ten-year-old who had been confined to a wheelchair pretty much since he was born. He suffered from hemimelia, a condition which meant that his legs didn’t fully develop below the knees. With the help of Jumping Kids, a non-profit organisation which helps fit youngsters with prostheses, Mahlangu was given shiny new cheetah blades. As he was watching the London 2012 Paralympics, he was just learning to walk again. It took some effort – he needed assistance with learning how to balance, but as with everything Mahlangu has done so far in his young life, he learnt quickly. It took him just five days to master the blades. “I was just learning to walk (in 2012 during the London Paralympic Games),” Mahlangu told the Paralympic News Service. “I was so excited when I took my first step that I vomited. The guy (doctor) asked me why I vomited and I told him I was so happy. I learnt fast, in about five days.” Five days after being able to walk, he could run. Since that day, Mahlangu has done nothing but excel. In 2014, he won gold in the National Athletics Championships and took silver in the long jump to boot. He set three new African records (and unofficial Junior World records) in the T42 under-20 category at the 2015 SASAPD National Athletics Championships and won gold in the javelin item. He competed against able-bodied athletes and set an unofficial (the record did not stand because it was against able-bodied athletes) senior record in the T42 400m in 2015. This year, he set the 400m T42 World Record (53.19s) to add to his African records in the 100m (13.34s), 200m (26.20s) and, unofficially, the 800m (2:14.00s). At the 2016 IAWS U23 World Games in June/July this year, he won gold in the T42 200m (25.89s), gold and beat his own world record in the 800m (2:06.70s), he also won gold in the 100m (13.13s), and won gold and beat his own world record in the 400m (52.61s). Before the Olympics, he won silver with a new personal best time of 23.97 at the Muller Anniversary Games in London in July. The silver at the Paralympics was yet another personal best and another African record, even if the 200m isn’t his preferred race. It is almost impossible not to be enchanted by this young, beaming, bouncing athlete. Prior to being fitted with prostheses he was in a school for disabled students, but has since moved to a different school – and adapted from English to Afrikaans as a medium of instruction. He dreams of being an engineer one day, because he doesn’t believe athletics should ever be work. He is wise beyond his young years and talented beyond words.
